TL;DR: the hour before bed matters more than total screen time. In a 2025 study of 1,200 kids aged 6 to 9, those on a screen in the last 60 minutes fell asleep about 19 minutes later, worst with handhelds held close to the face and games, mildest with a shared TV or a calm documentary. What helped: a fixed screens-off time an hour before bed every night including weekends, devices charging in the kitchen, and a choice of two books instead of haggling over minutes, with sleep onset back to normal within two weeks.
Action: Nothing else needed; copy this straight into the group chat if you want.

Rough rule of thumb: a retention curve has flattened when the period-over-period drop stays small, for example under 1 to 2 percentage points for three or more consecutive periods, so the line runs almost parallel to the x-axis. It's more convincing if the plateau holds across several cohorts and the cohorts are big enough that it isn't noise. The exact threshold depends on your cadence, so define it up front (less than X points per week for N weeks) and use it consistently.
Action: If you share the curve or the numbers, I'll check it against that rule.

EFT is the broad term for electronic bank-to-bank transfers in Canada, typically batched, low cost and settling in a day or two (payroll deposits, pre-authorized debits). A wire is a single, individually sent, usually higher-value payment, often same day, with a higher fee and much harder to reverse. A wire is technically a kind of electronic transfer, but for merchant payouts they differ in speed, cost and reversibility, so sales shouldn't swap them.

Short answer: no, damage deposits aren't allowed in Ontario. A landlord can only take a last month's rent deposit, and for damage beyond normal wear the landlord has to apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board, not deduct it. Scuffed walls are usually normal wear, and if Diego paid a separate deposit he can ask for it back, or file a T1 application with the LTB within a year of moving out.
Action: Pull together a plain-language summary and the CLEO page for you to send Diego.

A heat warning means two or more days of very high heat are expected, and an extended heat warning means three or more days. In southern Ontario the trigger is roughly daytime highs of 31, overnight lows of 20 or more, or a humidex of 40 or higher. Same precautions either way, just plan for more hot nights in a row with an extended one.
